newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Kenya sees lower interest rates by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees lower interest rates by year-end.

text.p: Kenya's interest rates should ease by the end of this year, Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said on Thursday.
Mudavadi, in an interview with Reuters, also said that Kenya's economic reforms were mostly on target but the government had no plans for an early end to limits on foreign investment.

"We hope that by the end of the year the rate (on Treasury bills) will be down to 18 percent," he said during a Commonwealth finance ministers meeting in Bermuda. The rate is currently around 21 percent.
Mudavadi acknowledged that some reforms which needed parliamentary approval -- such as in pensions and telecommunications -- would take a little longer but on the whole there was progress.
He pointed to the budget deficit, the trade position, reserves and debt servicing as all areas where the country was fairly secure.
The government was also taking measures to make sure that next year's election would not throw the economy off track, such as placing limits on the amount it could borrow from the central bank.
"That is a very strong indication that we want to contain the destabilising effects of the election," he said.
The government is looking at further tax cuts but warned Kenyans not to expect too much to be done at once.

Commenting on pension reform, Mudavadi expected privatisation of the state NSSF pension agency to go to parliament by the end of November. He denied this issue was a source of friction with the International Monetary Fund.
Once next year's election is out of the way, private capital inflows should pick up, though he added the stock exchange did need to be more vigorous.
There were no plans to increase the 40 percent limit of foreign investment in listed companies, he said, even though confidence in the country was on the rise.
"To increase we would need time," he said. Further liberalisation was important but the inflow of capital could have negative impact.
